full_judgment:
This Rule has arisen out of a suit for Partition and is directed against an order passed by the First Court of Munsif, Sadar, Chittagong rejecting an application of the petitioner (who was Defendant MNo.9 in the said suit) in which he prayed for rejection of the plaintiff's application for the final decree. 

 2. The suit for Partition was instituted in 1958 and the plaintiff opposite parties Nos. 1 and 2 prayed for partition of the properties in the suit claiming 4 annas 18 gondas share therein. The learned Munsif decreed the suit in part in a preliminary form on 7-9-60 allowing 3 annas 17 gondas and 9 krant share to the plaintiffs. The plaintiffs preferred an appeal being Partition Appeal No. 297 of 1960 against the said decree to the Court of the District Judge, Chittagong and the appeal was allowed. Against the appellate decree the present petitioner and Defendant No. 8 preferred a Second Appeal to the High Court being Second Appeal No. 207 of 1962 which was dismissed on 27-7-66. 

 3. It appears that Defendant No. 8, Defendant No. 12 and Defendant No. 21 died on 5-11-64, 13-9-64 and 20-3-64 respectively during the pendency of the appeal in the High Court but no substituting of the heirs of the said deceased defendants was made in the Second Appeal. After the disposal of the Second Appeal and the arrival of the records in the trial Court, Plaintiffs filed on 13-3-67 an application for final decree and also an application for substitution of the heirs of the deceased defendants as named above, and the said heirs were substituted by an order of the learned Munsif on 6-4-67. 

 4. The petitioner has thereafter filed a petition for rejecting the plaintiffs' application for final decree, on the ground that there having been no substitution within 90 days from the death of the deceased defendants the suit for Partition has abated and therefore the application for final decree is not maintainable. It has also been stated in the said petition that all the heirs of Defendant No. 8 have not been brought on record. 

 5. The learned Munsif relying upon a decision of the Judicial Committee of the Privy Council in the case of Lakshmi Narayan Marwary and others Vs. Balmakund Marwary and another, reported in 51 Indian Appeal 321 same case A.I.R. 1924 Privy Council 198 same case 29 C.W.N. 391 and also a Division Bench Decision of the Calcutta High Court in the case of Bhusan Chandra Mondal Vs. Chhabimoni Dasi and others reported in A.I.R. 1948 Calcutta page 363 same case 53 C.W.N. 582 has taken the view that there could not be any abatement of a suit for partition on account of death of a party after a preliminary decree has been passed. 

 8. Mr. Mofakhar the learned Advocate appearing for the opposite parties on the other hand has contended that after the Privy Council, decision in Lakshmi Narain Marwarys case the concensus of the judicial opinions in the Indian Subcontinent has been that after a preliminary decree has been passed there cannot be any abatement of the suit although a discordant note was expressed by Mr. Justice Solaiman when he was in the Allahabad High Court, and in support of his contention he has relied upon a full Bench decision of the Madras High Court in the case of Perumal Pillai Vs. Perumal Chetty and others reported in 51 Mad. 701 same case A.I.R. 1928 Madras 914, a Division Bench Decision of the Calcutta High Court in the case of Bhusan Chandra Mondal Vs. Chhabimoni Dasi reported in A.I.R. 1948 Cal. 363 same case 53 C.W.N. 582, a Division Bench decision of the Patna High Court in the case of Babuie Shanti Devi Vs. Khodai Prosad Singh and others reported in A.I.R. 1942 Patna 430 and also the Privy Council decision in Lakshmi Narain Marawary's case. 

 9. The Privy Council decision cited by the learned Advocate for the petitioner (17 I.A. 150) does not relate the question which is before us. In that case a preliminary decree in a partition suit was passed against some defendants in the suit but on the death of a certain defendant before the final decree was passed on substitution was made and a final decree was obtained without bringing the legal representatives of the deceased defendant on record. Thereafter execution of the said decree having been started against the legal representatives of the said deceased defendant, an objection was taken that the operative decree having been obtained in the absence of the said representative after the death of his predecessor, the execution could not proceed against him. The Judicial committee upholding the objection of the legal representative made the following observation : 

 "An operative decree, obtained after the death of a defendant, by which the extent and quality of his liability, already declared in general terms, are for the first time ascertained, cannot bind the representatives of the deceased, unless they were made parties to the suit in which it was pronounced." 

 10. The above noted observation points out the lacuna in the decree passed against a deceased patty without bringing his legal representatives on record but does not deal with question whether the said legal representative can be substituted in place of the deceased defendant before the operative decree has been passed, even though an application for substitution has not been made within the usual period of limitation as prescribed for an application for substitution. 

 11. The case of Lakshmi Narayan Marwary and others, arose out of a Partition suit in which the trial court took the view that certain defendant was separated and therefore he was dismissed from the suit. An appeal was taken to the High Court of Patna which was compromised on certain terms. The suit was thereupon remitted to the Court of the Subordinate Judge for partition of the undivided property and also for the valuation of the share of the separated member. Thereafter a date was fixed for taking necessary step but the plaintiff having been absent the Subordinate Judge dismissed the suit for want of further prosecution. The High Court in exercise of its power under section 115 of the Code set aside the said order of the Subordinate Judge and restored the case to file. Lord Phillimore in delivering the judgment made the following observation : 

 "After a decree has once been made in a suit, the suit cannot be dismissed unless the decree is reversed in appeal. The parties have, on the making of the decree, acquired rights or incurred liabilities which are fixed, unless or until the decree is varied or set aside" 

 12. In the case of Aamol Singh and others Vs. Hari Shankar reported in A.I.R. 1930 All. page 910, in a mortgage suit, the question arose as to whether after the passing of the preliminary decree a mortgage suit could abate on account of the death of a defendant. Reliance having been placed on behalf of the appellant on the Privy Council decision in Lakshmi Narayan Marawary's case Solaiman, J. (as he then was) tried to distinguish the said Privy Council decision on the facts of the case and expressed the view that the Subordinate Judge in that case dismissed the suit under Order 17 rule 2 of the Code and that the observation of the Judicial Committee that a suit cannot be dismissed until the decree is reversed on appeal is applicable to a compromise decree as had been passed between the parties of the said suit. The learned Judge was of the opinion that there was nothing in the Privy Council case which could be taken to mean that all previous decisions of Indian Courts had been over-ruled and held that the provision of Order 22 rules 3 and 4 of the Code applied even after the passing of the preliminary decree. The same View was reiterated by the learned Judge as the acting Chief Justice of the Allahabad High Court in the Full Bench case of Mahabir Singh Vs. Tewari and others, reported in A.I.R. 1931 All. 490. 

 13. In the case of Janaki Nath Singa Roy Vs. Nirod Baran Roy and others reported in A.I.R. 1930 Cal. 422, a Division Bench of the Calcutta High Court took the view that after the passing of a preliminary decree in a suit for mesne profits and possession the provision of Order 22, rule 9 would be applicable in case of the death of the defendant. The Privy Council decision does not appear to have been cited before the learned Judges for their consideration nor does their attention appear to have been drawn to the earlier decision of the same High Court which, following the Privy Council decision has taken the view that the rule of abatement does not apply in such a case. A contention was made before the said Bench relying upon a Privy Council decision in the case of Kedarnath Goenka Vs. Anat Prosad Singh and others reported in A.I.R. 1925 Privy Council 117 same case 52 Indian Appeal 188 that the proceeding for ascertaining mesne profits after a preliminary decree had been passed in the suit was a matter for execution prove-ceding and as such the provisions of Order 22 of the Civil Procedure Code had no application and the learned Judges distinguished the said Privy Council case on the view that the decree considered by the Judicial Committee was passed when the old Code of 1882 had been in force and under the said Code the ascertainment of the quantum of mesne profits was a matter to proceed with in execution and therefore the rule as regards abatement of suit did not apply to that matter. 

 14. In the Sind case of Tulsidas Vs. Ramxan Abdullah, 1926. Sind 20, the rule of abatement was applied in a suit for mesne profits after a preliminary decree had been passed without noticing the Privy Council decision in Lakshmi Narayan Marowary's case. 

 15. On a perusal of the decision in the case of Lakshmi Narayan Marwari it does not appear that the Judicial Committee have rested their decision on the special facts of the case that the rights of the parties were ascertained on the basis of a compromise. It is clear that what was settled and compromised in the said case was the share of the plaintiffs and the partition of the undivided properties was to be made in further proceeding in the suit in the same way as in the case of a contested preliminary decree. The ratio decidendi is that when a certain decree has been passed finally determining certain rights and liabilities of the parties the suit cannot be dismissed unless the decree which has been passed is reversed on appeal or revision. This proposition is not peculiar to a compromise decree but is also effective in case of a contested or exparte preliminary decree. 

 16. On an examination of the terms of Order 22,rule 3 or 4 of the Code of Civil Procedure it would be clear that the said provisions are not to be attracted in a case where a decree has already been passed. What has been, provided in the said rules is that when there is a right to sue but such a right does not survive in favour of the surviving plaintiff or plaintiffs or against the surviving defendant or defendants, there is a question of abatement of the suit in default of an application for substitution made within the time prescribed therefore. But if there has already been a decree determining the rights of the parties finally there is no question of any right to sue surviving. The right to sue has already culminated and merged into a decree of the court and the suit has also come to an end to the said extent. 

 17. It may be that some of the rights which flow the decree already made are still to be ascertained by working out the said decree, but the basic rights have already been determined, and therefore there is no question of any further rights to sue existing. 

 Before the Privy Council decision in Lakshmi Narayan Marawary's case the Calcutta High Court held in two cases, viz. Bhut Nath Jana Vs. Tarachand Jana, 25 C.W.N. 595 same case A.I.R. 1921 Cal. 551, and Manujendra Datta Vs. Jnan Ranjan, A.I.R. 1926 Cal. 368, that the rule of abatement would apply even after the passing of a preliminary decree, . After the said Privy Council decision, a Full Bench of Madras High Court in the case of Perumal Pillai Vs. Perumal Chetty, A.I.R. 1928 Mad. 914. same case I.L.R. 51 Mad, 71 held following thy said Privy Council decision that the provisions of Order 22, rules 3 & 4, Civil Procedure Code did not apply to cases of death after the of preliminary decree. A Division Bench of the Calcutta High Court in the case of Nazir Ahammad Vs. Tamijuddin Ahammad, A.I.R. 1929 Cal.430, same case 57 Cal. 285 expressly held that the earlier decisions of the said High Court applying the rule of abatement to the case of the said High Court applying the rule of abatement to the case of death after preliminary decree were no longer good law in view of the observations made by the Privy Council. Similar views were expressed in the cases of Harihar Prosad Vs. Umesh Chandra, 37 C.W.N. 812 same case A.I.R. 1933 Case 798 and Priyabala Davi Vs. Sarajee Bala, A.I.R. 1936 Cal. 540. 

 18. The Calcutta High Court has reiteraated the same view in the case of Bhusan Chandra Mondal Vs. Chhabimoni Dasi and others reported in A.I.R. 1948 Cal. 363 same case 53 C.W.N. 582, and has held that the rule of abatement is not applicable in case of death of a party in a suit taking place after a preliminary decree has been passed and in such a case the provision of Order 22 rule of the Civil Procedure for which no period for limitation is provided will be applicable. Similar view has been taken by a Division Bench of Bombay High Court in the case of Dawarali Jafarali Saiyad Vs. Bai Jadi and others reported in A.I.R. 1940 Bombay 318, Full Bench of Nagpur High Court in the case of Bapu Vs. Gulabchand and others in A.I.R. 1929 Nagpur, 142, a Division Bench of Lahore High Court in the case of Rahim Baksha and others Vs. Walaiti Ram and another reported in A.I.R. 1930 Lahore 329, a Division Bench of Patna High Court in the case of Shanti Devi Vs. Khodai Prosad Singh, in A.I.R. 1940 Pat. 340, Division Bench of Lucknow High Court in the case of Mt. Lakhapati Kuar Vs. Daulat Singh A.I.R. 1927 Oudh 156 and a Division Bench of Rangoon High Court in the case of Muthiah Chettyar Vs. Than Zan A.I.R. 1933 Rang 318. 

 20. It will thus appear, on a consideration of the judicial authorities referred to above, that, whatever divergence there had been in judicial opinions in respect of applications of the rules relating to abatement after a preliminary decree has been passed, all the High Courts have, by and by, reached a consensus, after the Privy Council decision in Lakshmi Narayan Marawary's case. It is interesting to notice that after the Allahabad High Court had laid down in the Division Bench decision in A. I. R. 1930 All. 779 and also the Full Bench decision in A.I.R. 1931 All. 490 in no uncertain terms that the rule of abatement would apply even in a case in which a preliminary decree had been passed, the Allahabad High Court has amended rule 12 of Order 22 of the Code of Civil Procedure and the amended rule so far as Allahabad High Court is concerned, stands in the following form : 

 "Nothing in rules 3, 4 and 8 shall apply to proceedings in execution of a decree or order, or to a proceedings in the original court taken after the passing of the preliminary decree where a final decree also requires to be passed, having regard to the nature of the suit." 

 21. I find myself in respectful agreement with this judicial view that after preliminary decree has been passed settling the rights of the parties finally there can be no dismissal or abatement of a suit and as such the provision of Order 22 rule 4 of the Code of Civil Procedure is not applicable to the death of the party in such a case. The learned Munsif was quite right in substituting the heirs of the deceased defendant before the passing of the final decree and rejecting the application of the petitioner.
